synthesis: The logarithmic prime partition produces matched-variance scale increments whose two-point covariance changes with spatial separation. That covariance law supports a coarse shared-ancestry representation and, after truncated transform control and inversion, yields two complementary pair estimates: asymptotic factorization when every retained block has decorrelated and a covariance-sensitive once-versus-twice large-deviation cost for nearby points. Applying those estimates to the same grid of high-block events is what makes the second-moment existence argument work.
source_support: Unit u07 defines the logarithmic prime ranges, establishes roughly equal interior-block variances, and excludes the anomalous edge blocks. Units u05 and u13 respectively formulate the coarse tree bookkeeping and derive the scale-dependent two-point covariance from prime sums and bounded mixed moments. Unit u14 promotes those moments to cutoff Fourier-Laplace transforms; u15 converts partial correlation into the near-pair cost; u16 proves far-pair tail factorization after covariance cross terms become negligible; and u17 uses precisely that far/near split in the grid second moment to obtain a high point.
nonparaphrase_operation: Compose an arithmetic scale decomposition, a spatial-covariance-to-ancestry change of representation, and correlation-sensitive rare-event estimates into the dependence bookkeeping required by a second-moment count. No single parent supplies this full bridge from prime blocks to the existence argument.
limits: The tree is an approximate fixed-K model and not an identification of zeta with a branching random walk. The first and last prime blocks are discarded; moment matching, transform inversion, decorrelation, and factorization hold only in their stated parameter and separation ranges. Formula-dense thresholds, constants, exponents, and several extracted symbols remain source-image-sensitive, and the synthesis neither derives a full limiting law nor treats nearby blocks as literally identical or late blocks as exactly independent.
quality_reason: Accepted because distinct parent sections jointly establish a concrete dependency chain from prime-scale covariance through near/far pair estimates to second-moment control, while the synthesis preserves the approximation, cutoff, and OCR-sensitive proof burdens instead of promoting the tree analogy to an exact causal model.

synthesis: The same deterministic interval Sobolev inequality is reused with two different analytic inputs. For the zeta function it turns endpoint and derivative-product integrals into a coarse probabilistic upper bound for the short-interval supremum; for the mollified error zeta times M minus 1 it turns an existing mean-square approximation into uniform control throughout a typical short interval, with product differentiation generating the new derivative-moment obligations.
source_support: Unit u06 proves the supremum bound by applying the Sobolev inequality to zeta and controlling its endpoint and derivative terms with Chebyshev, Cauchy-Schwarz, and second moments of zeta and zeta-prime. Unit u10 explicitly invokes the same inequality for zeta M minus 1, starts from the preceding L2 mollification estimate, and controls the derivative zeta-prime M plus zeta M-prime using repeated Cauchy-Schwarz, fourth moments for zeta and zeta-prime, and mean-value bounds for M and M-prime.
nonparaphrase_operation: Abstract the common continuum-to-integral bridge and compare how changing the function from zeta to a mollified error changes the analytic proof obligations: the same supremum mechanism persists, while the product rule forces separate moment control for both factors and their derivatives. That transfer is visible only by relating the two units.
limits: This is structural reuse, not a black-box bound for arbitrary approximants. Each application depends on object-specific moment estimates; both conclusions are probabilistic over interval centers, the zeta bound is deliberately coarse, and the mollifier conclusion is on the shifted line and does not provide deterministic pointwise inversion. Exact powers, derivative marks, and logarithmic exponents are extraction-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted because the two units independently instantiate the identical deterministic bridge on different functions and jointly expose a concrete invariant mechanism together with the changed derivative-moment burden; the relation is more than a shared theme or paraphrase.
